newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian firms' profits seen squeezed in 1996/97-poll.
newsitem.headline: Indian firms' profits seen squeezed in 1996/97-poll.

text.p: Weak demand and rising costs will squeeze profit growth of top Indian firms in 1996/97 (April-March) with some sectors like cement and steel showing lower earnings, a Reuter poll showed on Monday.

Analysts' earnings forecasts for 28 firms on benchmark Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) top-30 index showed average net profit growth falling sharply to 5.9 percent from about 25 percent in 1995/96 and 32 percent in 1994/95.
The remaining two companies in the BSE index, Ranbaxy Laboratories and Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd, were left out of the survey because they had already posted their results.
Twenty-eight leading securities and brokerage houses participated in the poll.

Profit of state-run Steel Authority of India Ltd, the country's largest steel maker, was forecast to fall 33.2 percent to 8.87 billion rupees in 1996/97 against a growth of 19.9 percent to 13.29 billion a year ago.
"Sluggish demand and higher input costs like that of coal, power and freight were the chief causes," said Rajiv Saxena, research head at Lazard Credit Capital Research.
"I don't see any change in the current year," he said. "Any price increases would only help absorb additional costs."

Easier availability of funds, lower interest costs and a growth-oriented budget that cut tariffs and taxes but awaits parliament approval are seen helping companies this year, but the benefits will take time to become manifest.

Prime lending rates of Indian banks have fallen to 14 percent -- the lowest in two years -- after the central bank loosened purse strings a week ago in its credit and monetary policy for the first half of fiscal 1997/98.
"The revival of demand depends on many things," said an analyst with a local brokerage. "This could happen only towards the end of the first half (of fiscal 1997/98)."
Analysts forecast Associated Cement Companies profits would tumble 58 percent to 951.37 million rupees in 1996/97 due to poor realisations.

A fall in world polymer prices would hit petrochemical companies and though an improvement in market conditions is not seen, higher sales volumes are likely to drive profits higher in the year to March 31, 1998, analysts said.
One analyst forecast the profit of petrochemicals giant Reliance Industries to fall 7.6 percent to 12.06 billion rupees, then rebound 50 percent in 1997/98.
"Reliance will benefit from a phenomenal growth in capacities till 1999," he said.

In the auto sector, truck maker Tata Engineering and Locomotive Company profits are seen 28.7 percent higher at 6.82 billion rupees while tractor and utility vehicles manufacturer Mahindra & Mahindra's profits are forecast to rise 23.7 percent to 2.08 billion rupees.
Profits of State Bank of India, the country's largest commercial bank, are slated to jump 66 percent to 13.8 billion rupees.

Telephone monopoly Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd could see its profits grow 22.2 percent to 8.9 billion rupees and oil refiner Hindustan Petroleum Corp's profits are seen up 19.7 percent at 6.1 billion rupees, the poll showed.
Multinational detergents maker Hindustan Lever's profits are projected to rise 22.7 percent to 5.08 billion rupees in calendar 1997 and Glaxo's by 27.7 percent to 611.7 million rupees in 1997.
Analysts forecast profits of tobacco conglomerate ITC, in which B.A.T Industries Plc holds about one-third equity, to jump 42.4 percent to 3.7 billion rupees. ($1 = 35.76 rupees)
